content.text: The text combines several works. One essay defends Jewish distinctiveness, emancipation, and possible national restoration while opposing prejudice and urging national excellence. A long archaeological account argues—largely through speculative linguistic and cultural parallels—that the Maya influenced or shared origins with civilizations across Asia, Egypt, Africa, and Europe; it describes Yucatán, Chichén-Itzá, Uxmal, Chaacmol’s tomb, and Maya religion, language, astronomy, and customs. “Arne” follows a Norwegian farmer’s son shaped by poverty, parental conflict, guilt, music, and longing to travel over the mountains. After his father dies, Arne reconciles with his mother, falls in love with Eli, remains at Kampen, and marries her, while Eli’s parents also reconcile. A final natural-history passage describes the author’s insect-rich harmas near Sérignan and nocturnal frogs, owls, grasshoppers, crickets, and other wildlife.
